Here are two high-quality options:

---

### Option 1: Eloquent & Professional Prose (Recommended for clarity)

> Whoever comes to prepare my body for burial, do not disturb or question the delicate wreath of hair bound around my arm. You must leave this mysterious token untouched, for it serves as my outward soul—a deputy to the spirit that, once departed for heaven, leaves this strand behind to govern my body and preserve my limbs from decay. 
> 
> After all, if the delicate nervous system stemming from my own brain can hold my physical form together, then these strands—which grew from a far superior mind—are even more capable of preserving me. Unless, perhaps, she intended for this token to signify my torment, binding me as manacles shackle a prisoner condemned to die. 
> 
> Whatever her true intention, bury it alongside me. As a martyr for love, I fear that if these remains fell into other hands, they might inspire idolatry. Just as it was an act of humility on my part to attribute soul-like power to her hair, it is now an act of quiet defiance that, since she refused to accept all of me, I take a piece of her to the grave with me.

---

### Option 2: Refined Poetic Verse (Preserves the poetic structure)

> Whoever comes to wrap me in my shroud,  
> Do not disturb or question overmuch  
> This subtle wreath of hair upon my arm;  
> This sacred sign and secret, do not touch.  
> For ’tis my outward soul,  
> A viceroy to the spirit that, when flown  
> To heaven, leaves this token to control  
> And keep my physical frame from breaking down.  
> 
> For if the slender threads my brain extends  
> Can bind my limbs and make my body whole,  
> These strands that grew above a finer mind  
> Possess far greater power to control—  
> Unless she meant that I  
> Should read in this the emblem of my pain,  
> Bound like a manacle on a condemned man  
> Who waits in silence to be slain.  
> 
> Whatever her intent, bury it with me,  
> Lest as love’s martyr, it should spur devotion,  
> Breeding idolatry if other hands  
> Should claim these relics with unfair emotion.  
> And as it showed humility in me  
> To grant this hair the powers of a soul,  
> It shows some quiet courage now to know:  
> Though she rejected me, I bury part of her below.

---

### Key Information Retained:
* **Stanza 1:** The request to leave the bracelet of hair on the arm untouched, as it acts as a secondary "soul" keeping the body intact after death.
* **Stanza 2:** The logic comparing the brain's nerves to the superior power of her hair, alongside the alternative interpretation that the hair is a manacle symbolizing his condemnation.
* **Stanza 3:** The instruction to bury the hair to prevent it from becoming a holy relic (idolatry), concluding with the irony that while accepting the hair was humble, taking a piece of her to the grave after being rejected is an act of defiance.

As he prepares for his impending death, the speaker leaves strict instructions for those charged with dressing his corpse: they must neither disturb nor question the intricate wreath of hair bound around his arm. To him, this lock of his beloved’s hair is far more than a simple keepsake; it serves as a metaphysical safeguard. He conceives of it as an "outward soul"—a divine surrogate that will remain behind to shield his physical remains from corruption and decay long after his own true soul has departed for heaven.

The speaker contemplates the true purpose behind this mysterious token, oscillating between two starkly different interpretations. On one hand, he imagines the hair was bestowed upon him to bind his fragile physical frame together with a superior, elevated spiritual strength. On the other, he darkly muses that it may have been given as a manacle—a tragic symbol of his agonizing and unceasing captivity in the thrall of unrequited love. 

Regardless of its original intent, the speaker remains adamant that this hair must be interred alongside him in the earth. He strictly forbids its removal to prevent it from falling into the hands of the living, fearing that superstitious onlookers might mistake it for a sacred relic and wrongly elevate it to an object of holy worship. 

Yet, beneath these spiritual concerns lies a deeply personal and defiant motivation. Having endured the agonizing pain of unrequited affection, insisting on being buried with a physical part of his lover allows the rejected speaker to perform a final act of quiet rebellion. By carrying a piece of her with him into the silence of the grave, he achieves a strange, paradoxical form of possession—claiming in death the closeness he was denied in life.

Whoever you may be that comes at last to wash my cold flesh, wrap me in linen, and prepare my corpse for the dark earth, hear my strict command: do not touch the wreath of hair bound about my arm. Leave it undisturbed, just as it rests upon my skin. Look upon that woven ringlet with quiet awe, but let no curious finger pry it loose or seek to untie what she hath bound.

Pause, then, and consider what this delicate loop of hair signifies, for even in death my mind wrestles with its true nature. Is it a mystery of divine grace, an artificial soul sent by my beloved to preserve this ruin of a body? Hair, unlike frail flesh and crumbling bone, resists the corrupting touch of the grave; it does not decay. Perhaps she intended this golden or shadowy thread to act as a celestial anchor, radiating a subtle warmth to keep my scattered limbs together and guard my memory against total oblivion. If so, it is a holy talisman, a thread of life woven by her hand to sustain me even when breath has fled.

And yet, my bitter thoughts turn to a darker truth. Was this braid given not out of mercy, but out of cruel disdain? Look upon it not as a sacred soul, but as a manacle—a fetter fashioned from her own body to mark me as her condemned prisoner. I died of her coldness, executed by her unrelenting refusal to love me. What is this wreath, then, if not the very chain that dragged me to my doom? She bound my spirit while I lived, and now her lock remains upon my dead arm, a visible symbol of my bondage and her tyranny. 

Whether it be a soul that saves or a shackle that slays, let it be buried with me in the dark silence of the tomb. Do not leave it above ground where the living might gaze upon it. Should it remain in the light of day, foolish men would mistake it for a holy relic of some saint, falling to their knees to worship the hair of a woman who possessed no saintly pity. I will not have her cruelty canonized, nor will I allow others to adore the idol that destroyed me.

Therefore, bury it deep within the dust beside me. In this final act, my tragic devotion twists into a triumph of quiet malice. She denied me her love, her heart, and her body throughout my living days, keeping herself entirely out of my reach. But by taking this lock of hair into the grave, I drag a piece of her down into the dirt with me. Since she would not yield to me in life, I shall possess a fragment of her forever in death—a quiet, prideful defiance echoing from the shroud, ensuring that she, too, is buried in part alongside the man she broke.

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a classic Metaphysical poem about a lover being buried with a bracelet of hair as a relic.
counterfactuals.output:
The definitive poem for this is **"The Relique"** (The Relic) by the premier Metaphysical poet, **John Donne** (published posthumously in 1633). 

It features one of the most famous conceits in English literature: the image of a grave being reopened to find a skeleton wearing a **"bracelet of bright hair about the bone."** Donne imagines that future generations will mistake the lovers for saints and turn them into religious relics.

***

### **The Relique**
*by John Donne*

When my grave is broke up again
Some second time, to associate
With some woman, which there, by fate,
Hath preferences to lie,
(For I would have never thought to stay
Till doomsday, if I then see)
**A bracelet of bright hair about the bone,**
Will he not let us alone,
And think that there a loving couple lies,
Who thought that hearts could wear masks, such as eyes?

If this fall in a time, or land,
Where mis-devotion doth command,
Then, he that digs us up, will bring
Us, to the Bishop, and the King,
To make us **Reliques**; then
Thou shalt be a Mary Magdalen, and I
A something else thereby;
All women shall adore us, and some men;
And since at such time, miracles are sought,
I would have that age taught,
What miracles we harmless lovers wrought.

First, we loved well and faithfully,
Yet knew not what we loved, nor why;
Difference of sex no more we knew,
Than our Guardian Angels do;
Coming and going, we
Perchance might kiss, but not between those meals;
Our hands ne'er touched the seals,
Which nature, injured by late law, sets free;
These miracles we did; but now alas,
All measure, and all language, I should pass,
Should I tell what a miracle she was.

***

### Why it is a Classic Metaphysical Poem:
* **The Metaphysical Conceit:** Donne takes a gruesome, macabre image (a decaying skeleton with a ring of hair around the bone) and turns it into a tender symbol of immortal, spiritual love.
* **Blend of the Sacred and the Profane:** He elevates a romantic gift (the lover's hair) into a holy relic capable of working "miracles."
* **Witty Irony:** Donne pokes fun at religious superstition (calling future grave-robbers' worship "mis-devotion") while simultaneously asserting that his lady's pure love was a true earthly miracle. 

*(Note: Donne also explored a similar image in another famous poem, **"The Funeral,"** where he asks his shroud-makers not to remove the "subtle wreath of hair, which crowns my arm," calling it a charm to keep his body from decaying).*

Since you are focusing on **unrequited love** and **idolatry**, here are a few structural and thematic notes that might help your essay:

1. **The Language of Idolatry (Stanza 3):**
   * Donne explicitly uses the word **"idolatry"** and refers to the wreath of hair as a **"relic."** 
   * In Protestant post-Reformation England, venerating religious relics was viewed as idolatrous. Donne blends sacred Catholic imagery with profane/courtly love, treating the beloved like a deity whose physical token holds supernatural power.

2. **The Turn Toward Unrequited Love (Ending):**
   * Throughout the poem, the speaker frames the "wreath of hair" as a protective charm or a soul substitute. 
   * However, the final stanza introduces a shift in tone: he wonders if she gave it to him as a **"manacle"** (a symbol of imprisonment/rejection).
